At hatching, the wet weight of the nestling increases to around 0.65 grams [Wwb = around 0.65 grams], representing a modest gain during the brief internal incubation period. Eggs subjected to a controlled incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] yield hatchlings after a developmental interval of 16.5 days [ab = 16.5 days], a duration that aligns with values reported for other small-bodied Neotropical hummingbirds. The relatively short incubation period reflects the rapid embryonic differentiation characteristic of trochilids, where the yolk-dependent embryo must transition quickly to exogenous feeding. Once hatched, the altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning, and its initial mass underscores the energetic challenge facing both the brooded chick and its attending adults in the warm, humid lowland forests of Trinidad and Tobago, where this species is commonly encountered.

Fledging marks a critical developmental milestone for the altricial nestling, achieved at approximately 21 days after hatching [tx = approximately 21 days after hatching] when maintained at the typical active-body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. During this period, the chick undergoes rapid feather development and wing muscle strengthening, culminating in its first flight achievement and subsequent nest departure. The timing of fledging in Saucerottia tobaci is consistent with that observed in other medium-sized hummingbirds, reflecting a balance between the need for sufficient somatic growth and the pressures of nest predation. Following fledging, the immature individual enters a phase of nutritional independence onset, though it may still receive occasional provisioning from the adult female. The post-fledging dispersal phase is critical for juvenile survival, as young birds must learn to locate floral resources and defend feeding territories in a competitive environment. The fledgling precursor, now capable of sustained flight, gradually refines its foraging skills over subsequent weeks, a period that precedes the more energetically demanding stages of gonadal maturation and eventual recruitment into the breeding population.

Reproductive output in the Copper-rumped hummingbird is characterized by a consistent pattern of two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a modal value that appears invariant across much of its range. Breeding females are capable of producing approximately 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 clutches per year] under the thermal conditions typical of their tropical lowland habitat, where the ambient body temperature remains near 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This annual reproductive effort yields a maximum potential of five eggs per breeding season, a comparatively modest output that aligns with the life-history strategy of many Trochilidae. The duration of gonadal maturation in this species is brief relative to its total lifespan; puberty is attained at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], allowing young birds to become reproductively viable within a few months of fledging. This rapid sexual maturation contrasts with the slower pace observed in some temperate-zone hummingbirds, likely reflecting the reduced seasonality and abundant year-round nectar resources available to Saucerottia tobaci in its equatorial environment.

The onset of first breeding in Saucerottia tobaci occurs at approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], meaning that most individuals delay reproduction until their second calendar year. This age at first successful reproduction represents a strategic deferral that allows the juvenile to achieve asymptotic body size and establish a stable feeding territory before committing to the energetic demands of egg production and parental care. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 4.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 4.9 grams], a modest mass that places this species among the smaller members of the genus Saucerottia. The attainment of this adult body mass occurs gradually over several months following fledging, as the immature bird accumulates lipid reserves and develops the flight musculature required for efficient hover-feeding. Longevity data for the Copper-rumped hummingbird are derived primarily from comparisons with related species, as direct mark-recapture studies remain limited. The maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately ten years [am = approximately ten years] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature near 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a value extrapolated from well-documented records for the Black-chinned Hummingbird (Archilochus alexandri). Such a decadal lifespan (ten years) [am = ten years] is exceptional for a bird weighing less than 5 grams and reflects the exceptionally low extrinsic mortality rates that hummingbirds can achieve in predator-free or low-predation environments at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. The lifespan completion in Saucerottia tobaci is typically attributable to physiological senescence or stochastic environmental events rather than to predictable age-related organ failure, as hummingbirds do not display the dramatic reproductive senescence observed in some other avian lineages.
